items.title: Plus de 300 personnes témoignent d’une perte qui bouleverse leur vie
items.author: Elizabeth Gagné
items.excerpt: Une enquête québécoise menée auprès de 304 personnes endeuillées par suicide révèle les conséquences profondes de cette perte, mais aussi les lacunes dans les services de soutien offerts aux proches.
items.leadExcerpt: Le deuil à la suite d’un suicide laisse des traces qui peuvent persister pendant des années. À l’approche de la Journée internationale des personnes endeuillées par suicide, le 21 novembre, l’Association québécoise de prévention du suicide (AQPS), le Centre de recherche interdisciplinaire sur le suicide et ses enjeux éthiques (CRISE) et le Centre de prévention du suicide de Montréal (CPSM) dévoilent les premiers résultats d’une enquête menée auprès de 304 personnes ayant vécu cette épreuve au Québec.

items.title: En France, la colère lycéenne gagne tout le pays
items.author: Elise Miara
items.excerpt: Depuis près d’un mois, des lycéen·ne·s français·es bloquent leurs établissements scolaires et manifestent par centaines de milliers pour réclamer plus de professeur·e·s, des locaux dignes et une réforme de la plateforme Parcoursup. Né dans un lycée de la banlieue parisienne, le
items.leadExcerpt: Depuis près d’un mois, des lycéen·ne·s français·es bloquent leurs établissements scolaires et manifestent par centaines de milliers pour réclamer plus de professeur·e·s, des locaux dignes et une réforme de la plateforme Parcoursup. Né dans un lycée de la banlieue parisienne, le mouvement met le gouvernement sous pression, à six mois de la présidentielle. Tout a commencé le 17 septembre dernier au lycée Saint-Exupéry de Créteil, dans le Val-de-Marne, où des professeur·e·s faisaient grève contre des postes non pourvus. Les élèves ont ensuite bloqué l’établissement, et la contestation a rapidement gagné tout le pays. Le 6 octobre, 266 000 personnes ont défilé dans les rues de France, selon le ministère de l’Intérieur, 450 000 selon les organisateur·rice·s. Les parents d’élèves et le personnel enseignant soutiennent les jeunes dans leurs revendications, et des organisations plus traditionnelles des mouvements sociaux ont décidé de se joindre à la mobilisation, à l’image des syndicats de l’Éducation nationale et de partis politiques de gauche, comme La France insoumise (LFI).

items.leadExcerpt: Le drapeau de la Grande semaine des tout-petits a été hissé ce lundi devant l’hôtel de ville de Saguenay, pour lancer la 11e édition de cette mobilisation provinciale. L’événement veut rappeler l’importance d’investir tôt dans le développement et le bien-être des enfants de 0 à 5 ans. Organisée par le Collectif petite enfance, la campagne se poursuit jusqu’au 22 novembre sous le thème « Un grand Québec commence petit ». Elle mobilise plus de 375 municipalités et des milliers d’organisations à travers la province, qui lèvent simultanément le drapeau de l’événement pour afficher leur engagement envers les familles et l’égalité des chances.

items.title: The conditions of compassion
items.author: Théa Spoorenberg
items.excerpt: There is an unspoken hierarchy in the way we distribute sympathy. Some victims are immediately recognized as innocent, with their suffering understood as an injustice in itself, while others are met with suspicion, political scrutiny, or framed as matters of collective
items.leadExcerpt: There is an unspoken hierarchy in the way we distribute sympathy. Some victims are immediately recognized as innocent, with their suffering understood as an injustice in itself, while others are met with suspicion, political scrutiny, or framed as matters of collective responsibility. The difference is not necessarily the scale of suffering, but rather who is suffering, where they come from and what political circumstances surround them. Consider the international discourse surrounding Ukraine and Gaza. While both conflicts are historically and politically distinct, the language used to discuss their civilian populations raises an uncomfortable question: why are some victims so readily granted the benefit of innocence while others find their suffering qualified by political context?

items.title: Wicker: More Than Meets The Eye
items.author: Abby Schiff
items.excerpt: Wicker has had massive success in its opening, making back half of its budget in its first weekend in cinemas. With a whopping 94% on Rotten Tomatoes and 92% on the Popcornmeter, critics and audiences alike are clearly taking well to the movie.
items.imageCredit: Photo : Guilhermeduartegarcia / CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
items.leadExcerpt: Wicker has had massive success in its opening, making back half of its budget in its first weekend in cinemas. With a whopping 94% on Rotten Tomatoes and 92% on the Popcornmeter, critics and audiences alike are clearly taking well to the movie. Much of the marketing and social media coverage for the movie has been highly sexualized, focusing on actor Alexander Skarsgård’s portrayal of a hunky, anthropomorphic handicraft. The website Screenrant, for example, titled their piece on the film simply “Alexander Skarsgård’s New Fantasy Movie.” The movie’s promotion also leaned heavily on the sensationalism, releasing trailers which focalized the film’s handful of sex scenes. While this marketing has certainly been attention-grabbing, it has obscured the film’s deeper, more interesting messaging.

items.title: Documentary film ‘NAZA’ examines the banality of evil behind the horrific Gaza genocide
items.author: Cléo Clamen
items.excerpt: The film consists of 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers interviewed about the atrocities they have committed. The British documentary NAZA (which will begin streaming in late November) consists of interviews with Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers. The film
items.leadExcerpt: Each interviewee is shown only as a dark silhouette to protect their anonymity. This choice also turns them into a blank canvas for the audience to project onto. It demonstrates what can happen when ordinary people say nothing in the face of injustice, participate in gradually escalating and extraordinarily horrific acts of evil and ultimately become a complicit instrument of mass atrocity. The film’s title comes from the Hebrew ‘Nezek Agavi,’ a term used by the Israeli military to refer to civilian casualties. In an early scene, an intelligence officer described how the military refers to civilian casualties not as “15 women and children” or “15 people” but simply “15 NAZA.” NAZA is repeatedly discussed throughout the film as a “necessary loss” considered when the military decides whether or not to strike a building.

items.leadExcerpt: À l’âge de 10 ans, Jérémy Gagnon découvre le parkour dans une vidéo de l’acrobate Damien Walters et sait immédiatement qu’il veut en faire sa discipline. Aujourd’hui entraîneur à l’ACTN3 – Ninja Warrior & Parkour à Montréal, il enchaîne les figures acrobatiques en toute tranquillité. Derrière ce calme se cache pourtant une pratique où chaque mouvement doit être maîtrisé, afin d’éviter la moindre erreur. Quelques minutes avant l’ouverture d’ACTN3, à Montréal, la salle est encore silencieuse. Les tapis sont immobiles, les barres attendent les premier·ère·s pratiquant·e·s. Jérémy Gagnon, 25 ans, est déjà là. Calme et discret, il est loin de l’image spectaculaire que peut renvoyer le parkour.

items.title: Three arrested at anti-austerity student protest
items.author: Léo Vallet David
items.excerpt: Thousands of students protested on Friday over their discontent with austerity measures, eventually leading to three arrests and clashes with the police.
items.leadExcerpt: On Friday, Nov. 13, thousands of students rallied at Square-Victoria around 2 p.m. to protest austerity measures imposed on the province’s CEGEPs and universities. The crowd was estimated at between 75,000 and 100,000 people, according to reports from both La Presse and Radio-Canada. The SPVM did not calculate the exact number of protesters. The protest ended at around 5 p.m. with three arrests and eight mischiefs — a legal term describing property damage or destruction, property rendered dangerous, useless, inoperative or ineffective, obstructed, or interrupting or interfering with its lawful use — confirmed by the Montreal police (SPVM).

items.title: More than half of Quebecers are unsatisfied with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, according to recent poll
items.author: Léo Vallet David
items.excerpt: A recent Pallas Data poll puts St-Pierre Plamondon’s approval rating at 23 per cent, an unwelcome sign for a newly elected minority government
items.leadExcerpt: The results are even worse on the Island of Montreal, where the Parti Québécois (PQ) won two seats — including St-Pierre Plamondon’s. Only 14 per cent of of respondents were satisfied with his government, compared to 62 per cent who were not. In the greater Montreal area — which encompasses Laval, the north and south shores — that number goes down to 50 per cent saying they’re unsatisfied with the performance so far and 26 per cent said they’re satisfied. On Oct. 5, the PQ carried 26 ridings in both the north and south shores.

items.leadExcerpt: Deux ans après la création de Santé Québec, quoi garder et quoi réformer ? Ce qui s’annonçait comme un projet mettant à l’avant-plan l’efficience, semble pourtant ajouter un poids sur la bureaucratie dans un ministère déjà alourdi. Le premier ministre du Québec, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, avait promis d’abolir Santé Québec lors de la plus récente campagne. Ce dernier semble pourtant se rétracter et parle désormais d’une « réforme », en ne conservant que les éléments fonctionnels.

items.excerpt: As we enter November, I am confident that many McGillians share the dread I feel, knowing that the days of sitting on Lower Field with only a light sweater are behind us. As a Canadian, I don’t believe I will ever fully acclimatise to this weather, even two decades in. Facing
items.leadExcerpt: As we enter November, I am confident that many McGillians share the dread I feel, knowing that the days of sitting on Lower Field with only a light sweater are behind us. As a Canadian, I don’t believe I will ever fully acclimatise to this weather, even two decades in. Facing this impending drop in temperature and the relegation of warm weather to the realm of the fever dream, I decided a rewatch of Sterling Point (2026) was in order. How better to hold onto Canada’s summers than by climbing right back into that environment, letting this well-made, sunny, coming-of-age show take over my screen once again?

items.title: How a student-led movement prevailed in Serbia’s election
items.author: Léo Vallet David
items.excerpt: After months of protests and years of frustration, Serbian students have prevailed, electing 140 pro-student candidates to the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia on Oct. 25.
items.leadExcerpt: The newly created Student List (SL) party won 140 seats, while President Aleksandar Vučić’s United Serbia party won 103, giving the SL a majority of 30 seats in Serbia’s parliament. This shift in Serbian politics marks a new era, with young protesters having led the charge to remove Aleksandar Vučić from power. Vučić, who was Serbia’s prime minister from 2014 to 2017, was first elected president in 2017 with 56 per cent of the votes. He won the presidential election again in 2022, though his party narrowly lost its majority in parliament, which it won back in 2023.

items.title: Why young people should watch more films like Persepolis
items.author: Chloé Etienne
items.excerpt: As a Concordia student minoring in film studies, I am fortunate to have access to a wide range of films that enrich and educate me on a daily basis. During my film history class this week, I had the chance to watch Persepolis, a French animated film adapted from the
items.leadExcerpt: As a Concordia student minoring in film studies, I am fortunate to have access to a wide range of films that enrich and educate me on a daily basis. During my film history class this week, I had the chance to watch Persepolis, a French animated film adapted from the autobiographical graphic novel by Marjane Satrapi, a Franco-Iranian artist. Directed by Satrapi herself and Vincent Paronnaud, Persepolis explores Marjane’s childhood in Tehran, which is marked by the 1979 Islamic Revolution, the mullahs’ regime, the oppression suffered by women and the Iran-Iraq War. But beyond political and social issues, the film portrays resilience and the determination to push through and fight for one’s rights.
